subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a relative clause after "the only one of the [plural noun] that," where "one" is the antecedent, crossed with active vs. passive voice decided by a delayed object
passage: Many insects visit the trumpet-shaped flowers of sacred datura after dark, but most of them take nectar without picking up much pollen. In footage from the current flowering season at a single desert site, the white-lined sphinx moth is the only one of the regular nocturnal visitors that ______, on nearly every visit and in quantities large enough to matter, pollen from one plant's anthers to a neighboring plant's stigma.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Because of "the only," the relative pronoun "that" refers to "one" (the moth), not to "visitors": the moth is the single member of the group that does this, so the verb in the relative clause must be singular. The moth is also the one doing the carrying, and the thing carried, "pollen," appears later in the sentence as the verb's object, so the verb must be active: "is carrying." "are carrying" is active but plural, agreeing with "visitors" as if the clause described the whole group rather than the only one of them. "is carried" is singular but passive, which would make the moth the thing carried and leave "pollen" with no grammatical role. "are carried" is both plural and passive.
topic_tag: pollination ecology: hawk moths and night-blooming flowers

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in an it-cleft ("it is the [plural noun] ... that"), where the verb agrees with the clefted plural rather than with "it is," crossed with passive vs. active voice decided by meaning
passage: Freshwater mussels are notoriously hard to tell apart, because the shape of a shell changes with the speed of the water and the age of the animal. After reviewing a large museum collection, curators reported that it is the juvenile shells from fast-flowing headwater streams that ______ most often, since their thin, compressed valves closely resemble those of entirely different species.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: In a cleft sentence such as "it is the juvenile shells ... that," the verb in the "that" clause agrees with the noun that has been singled out, "the juvenile shells," not with the singular "it is" that introduces it, so the verb must be plural. The shells are also what the curators and earlier cataloguers get wrong; they do not identify anything themselves, and the clause names nothing that they would be misidentifying, so the verb must be passive: "are misidentified." "is misidentified" is passive but singular, agreeing with "it is" instead of with "shells." "are misidentifying" is plural but active, which would make the shells the ones doing the identifying and leaves the verb without the object it requires. "misidentifies" is both singular and active.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in an embedded "that" clause whose own singular subject sits right before the blank, after a long plural matrix subject, crossed with active vs. passive voice decided by a delayed object
passage: Leaf-out dates have been logged at botanical gardens for more than a century, and those records are now being mined to predict how forests will respond to warming. The botanists and climatologists who compiled four decades of these records from gardens across the temperate zone now argue that across those decades photoperiod ______, more decisively than spring warmth or soil moisture, the week in which beech buds finally open.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The verb belongs to the clause introduced by "that," whose subject is "photoperiod" (day length), a singular noun; the long plural subject of the main clause, "The botanists and climatologists ... ," goes with "argue," not with this verb. Photoperiod is also what does the determining, and what it determines, "the week in which beech buds finally open," follows the interrupting phrase as the verb's object, so the verb must be active, and the present perfect fits a pattern holding "across those decades" of records: "has determined." "have determined" is active but plural, agreeing with "botanists and climatologists." "is determined" is singular but passive, which would make photoperiod the thing determined and leave "the week" with no grammatical role. "are determined" is both plural and passive.

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a "more than one [singular noun]" subject, which takes a singular verb, crossed with simple past vs. present and present perfect decided by a distant "until" clause
passage: Sediment cores from deep lakes can preserve thousands of years of pollen, ash, and charcoal, but only if they come out of the ground intact. Until the field team switched to chilled drill bits, which now keep the mud frozen during extraction, more than one core from the lake's deepest basin ______ on arrival at the deck, with the layers smeared beyond reading.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: A subject of the form "more than one" plus a singular noun ("more than one core") takes a singular verb, even though it refers to several cores. The time frame is set by "Until the field team switched to chilled drill bits": the damage happened during a past period that ended with the switch, and the bits "now keep the mud frozen," so the problem no longer occurs. That calls for the simple past: "was in pieces." "is in pieces" is singular but present, describing a current state that the switch has ended. "has been in pieces" is singular but present perfect, which would stretch the damage up to the present, contradicting the past cutoff set by "until ... switched." "have been in pieces" has the same tense problem and is also plural, treating "more than one core" as plural.

subskill: form: auxiliary choice in a negative inversion ("Not until ... do/does/did") with a postposed plural subject whose head comes well after the blank, crossed with present tense set by the passage's other verbs
passage: Fairy shrimp spend their entire adult lives in desert rock pools that hold water for only a few weeks each year. Not until autumn rains refill the shallow basins worn into the sandstone ledges ______ tiny, thick-walled, and nearly indestructible resting eggs left behind in the dried silt hatch, sometimes after lying dormant for decades.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: After a fronted "Not until ..." phrase, the sentence inverts, and with a base-form main verb ("hatch") the inversion uses a form of "do" that agrees with the subject. That subject comes after the blank: its head is "eggs" ("the tiny, thick-walled, and nearly indestructible resting eggs"), which is plural. The passage describes a recurring natural cycle in the present tense ("spend," "hold," "refill"), so the auxiliary must be present and plural: "do the." "does the" is present but singular, as if the subject were singular. "did the" is past, which does not fit a cycle described in the present tense. "is the" cannot combine with the base form "hatch" at all; "is" would need a participle ("is ... hatching"), and it is also singular.
topic_tag: desert ecology: fairy shrimp in ephemeral pools

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a fronted participial inversion with a plural noun before the blank and a singular postposed subject, crossed with simple past vs. present and present perfect decided by a later present-perfect verb
passage: When a retired farmer donated a battered tin box to a regional seed library, the staff expected only seeds. The box held dozens of paper envelopes of bean and squash seed, each labeled in faded pencil. Bundled with the envelopes ______ the farmer's own handwritten account of how her family saved each variety for four generations, though it bore no signature; the library has since transferred it to the county archive for safekeeping.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: This sentence is inverted: it opens with "Bundled with the envelopes," and its subject follows the verb. The subject is "the farmer's own handwritten account," whose head "account" is singular, so the verb must be singular even though the plural "envelopes" comes just before the blank. The tense is set by what happened afterward: "the library has since transferred it to the county archive," so the account is no longer bundled with the envelopes, and the sentence must describe how the box was when it was donated ("The box held"). That calls for the past: "was evidently." "is evidently" is singular but present, claiming the account is still in the box, which the transfer rules out. "has evidently been" is singular but present perfect, which would extend the bundling up to the present, also ruled out by the transfer. "were evidently" is past but plural, agreeing with "envelopes."
topic_tag: seed saving: an heirloom seed library

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a "Such + be + subject + that" inversion with the subject head well after the blank, crossed with present perfect vs. past perfect and simple present decided by a distant "ever since" clause
passage: On the dry slopes of the island, the native juniper woodland has shrunk to a few stands clinging to cliffs. Such ______ the steady, year-round browsing pressure from free-ranging goat herds ever since farmers stopped penning their animals at night that almost no juniper seedling now survives past its first summer.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: In "Such ... that" sentences the verb comes before its subject. The subject here is "the steady, year-round browsing pressure," whose head "pressure" is singular; the plural nouns that follow ("goat herds," "farmers," "animals") belong to modifying phrases. The time frame is set by "ever since farmers stopped penning their animals," which describes a situation running from a past starting point up to the present, where seedlings "now" fail to survive; that requires the present perfect. So the answer is "has been." "have been" has the right tense but is plural, agreeing with "goat herds" instead of "pressure." "had been" is past perfect, which needs a later past moment to look back from, but the result is stated in the present ("now survives"). "is now" is present but cannot carry a span that began "ever since" a past event.
topic_tag: island ecology: goat browsing and juniper loss
